power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 30 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (30). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 819 columns across 19 data files.
#### Issues Identified

85 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 19 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: This study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines from (i) the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Review of Interventions (Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, 2008), and (ii) the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) (Liberati et al., 2009).
text.formatted: This study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines from (i) the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Review of Interventions (Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, 2008), and (ii) the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Liberati et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The global population is aging at an unprecedented rate, with the number of individuals aged 60 and older projected to double by 2050 (Navaneetham & Arunachalam, 2022).
text.formatted: The global population is aging at an unprecedented rate, with the number of individuals aged 60 and older projected to double by 2050 <ref type="bibr">(Navaneetham & Arunachalam, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This demographic shift demands urgent attention, particularly for middle-aged and older adults, who face escalating health challenges.
Aging is closely associated with an elevated risk of cognitive decline and a higher likelihood of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD).

Conditions such as cardiovascular diseases, mobility or balance impairments, and various cancers threaten older adults' autonomy, and quality of life (Logsdon et al., 2002; Mosti et al., 2019; Murman, 2015).
text.formatted: Conditions such as cardiovascular diseases, mobility or balance impairments, and various cancers threaten older adults' autonomy, and quality of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Logsdon et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Mosti et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Murman, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Age-related cognitive decline typically involves a progressive deterioration in domains such as processing speed, memory, attention, and executive functions (EFs).
Among these domains, EFs are particularly susceptible to the effects of aging and are among the earliest cognitive functions impaired in ADRD (Guarino et al., 2019; Hodges et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Among these domains, EFs are particularly susceptible to the effects of aging and are among the earliest cognitive functions impaired in ADRD <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Guarino et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Hodges et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Core EFs include (i) working memory (WM), a limited-capacity system responsible for temporary storage and manipulation of information (Conway et al., 2003), (ii) attentional control, which enables individuals to focus on goal-relevant information while limiting the interference of competing or distracting stimuli (Oberauer, 2019; Theeuwes, 2025), and (iii) cognitive flexibility, the capacity to shift attention efficiently across multiple tasks (Ionescu, 2012).
text.formatted: Core EFs include (i) working memory (WM), a limited-capacity system responsible for temporary storage and manipulation of information <ref type="bibr">(Conway et al., 2003)</ref>, (ii) attentional control, which enables individuals to focus on goal-relevant information while limiting the interference of competing or distracting stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Oberauer, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Theeuwes, 2025)</ref>, and (iii) cognitive flexibility, the capacity to shift attention efficiently across multiple tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Ionescu, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These functions are fundamental for higher-order cognitive processes such as reasoning, problem-solving, goal-directed behavior, and learning.
They also play a vital role in everyday functioning, influencing social interactions, emotional regulation, and mental health (Diamond, 2013; Zelazo & Carlson, 2012).
text.formatted: They also play a vital role in everyday functioning, influencing social interactions, emotional regulation, and mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Diamond, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Zelazo & Carlson, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Critically, the integrity of EFs has cascading effects on both functional independence and overall quality of life (Davis et al., 2010; Kudlicka et al., 2014; Logsdon et al., 2002).

text.text: Accordingly, there is an urgent need to develop cost-effective, scalable, and evidence-based interventions to mitigate the growing public health burden of cognitive decline and ADRD (Chowdhary et al., 2022).

text.text: Physical activity and exercise have been identified as promising approaches that meet the criteria outlined above (Haskell et al., 2007; Iso-Markku et al., 2024; Kramer et al., 1999; Voss et al., 2013), with meta-analytic evidence consistently demonstrating the positive impact of exercise on cognitive and brain health in older adults (Borges-Machado et al., 2021; Colcombe & Kramer, 2003; Gallardo-Gómez et al., 2022; Gheysen et al., 2018).

text.text: "Cognitive and brain health" refers to the optimal functioning of cognitive processes along with the structural and functional integrity of the brain (Gorelick & Sorond, 2024).
text.formatted: "Cognitive and brain health" refers to the optimal functioning of cognitive processes along with the structural and functional integrity of the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Gorelick & Sorond, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, age-related changes in these domains often begin in middle age, well before the clinical onset of dementia-related disorders (Bartrés-Faz et al., 2025; Dohm-Hansen et al., 2024).

text.text: While exercise interventions have demonstrated cognitive benefits in older adults, targeting middle adulthood could be especially critical, as this transitional stage may represent a window of opportunity during which early signs of decline first emerge (Livingston et al., 2024).

text.text: Similarly, training with action video games has been shown to positively affect both brain and cognitive function (Bediou et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Similarly, training with action video games has been shown to positively affect both brain and cognitive function <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bediou et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Building on evidence supporting the cognitive and brain benefits of exercise and certain types of cognitive training video games, recent findings highlight simultaneous perceptual cognitive-motor training (i.e., exercise that integrates physical and cognitive components), as one of the most effective strategies for maintaining or enhancing cognitive and brain health in middle-aged and older adults (Huang et al., 2022).

text.text: Exergaming refers to electronically powered, sensor-based interactive games that require whole-body, gross motor movements to interact with the game environment.

It represents a rapidly growing form of motor-cognitive training that allows individuals to engage in physical activity while responding to real-time digital feedback (Baranowski et al., 2008; Lu, 2015; Maddison, Ralph et al., 2013).
text.formatted: It represents a rapidly growing form of motor-cognitive training that allows individuals to engage in physical activity while responding to real-time digital feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baranowski et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Lu, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Maddison, Ralph et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These interactive experiences can be delivered through screen-based systems or immersive technologies such as head-mounted augmented or virtual reality (e.g., Azure Kinect; Meta Quest).

Exergame platforms span multiple technological generations that differ in interaction modes, and, accordingly, in the cognitive and motor demands placed on the players (Maggio et al., 2025; Torre & Temprado, 2022).
text.formatted: Exergame platforms span multiple technological generations that differ in interaction modes, and, accordingly, in the cognitive and motor demands placed on the players <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Maggio et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Torre & Temprado, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Early console-based exergames (e.g., dance mats and Nintendo Wii balance board games) tended to rely on discrete, prompt-driven inputs, which emphasized reaction timing and stimulus-response correspondence rather than whole-body control.

Later generations increasingly incorporated full-body motion tracking and more naturalistic interaction paradigms, thereby placing greater demands on sensorimotor coordination and attentional control.

For example, camera-based motion-capture systems (e.g., Microsoft Kinect) require whole-body movement and continuous spatial monitoring of the players' position relative to the targets on screen (van Diest et al., 2014).
text.formatted: For example, camera-based motion-capture systems (e.g., Microsoft Kinect) require whole-body movement and continuous spatial monitoring of the players' position relative to the targets on screen <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">(van Diest et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, handheld systems (e.g., Nintendo Wii) primarily rely on motion captured through handheld devices, with interaction largely mediated by upper-limb gestures and movement timing.
As a result, these systems tend to elicit lower levels of physical activity than camera-based platforms and thus require less energy expenditure (Marks et al., 2015).
text.formatted: As a result, these systems tend to elicit lower levels of physical activity than camera-based platforms and thus require less energy expenditure <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Marks et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: More recently, immersive virtual systems using head-mounted devices have introduced egocentric interaction, embodied navigation, and richer sensorimotor contingencies that are largely absent from conventional screen-based exergames, potentially increasing demands on spatial cognition and multisensory integration (Gittinger & Wiesche, 2024; Parsons, 2015).
text.formatted: More recently, immersive virtual systems using head-mounted devices have introduced egocentric interaction, embodied navigation, and richer sensorimotor contingencies that are largely absent from conventional screen-based exergames, potentially increasing demands on spatial cognition and multisensory integration <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Gittinger & Wiesche, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Parsons, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: From a human-computer interaction perspective, these shifts have changed how players interact with the system: early console-based exergames offered largely fixed, score-based feedback on a shared external display, whereas later camerabased and immersive head-mounted systems support richer, real-time, and increasingly adaptive feedback within a more egocentric interaction framework.
These design characteristics may enhance user engagement and shape the cognitive processes recruited during gameplay, with potential implications for training outcomes (Torre & Temprado, 2022).
text.formatted: These design characteristics may enhance user engagement and shape the cognitive processes recruited during gameplay, with potential implications for training outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Torre & Temprado, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Since these paradigms result in different demands on attention, executive function, postural control, spatial processing, and real-time motor adjustment, understanding their impact on cognitive and physical health requires a nuanced evaluation across technological platforms.

In the last decade, several meta-analyses have shown small-to-moderate positive effects of exergaming on cognitive outcomes in middle-aged and older adults (J. Y. C. Chan et al., 2024; Manser et al., 2024; Soares et al., 2021; Stanmore et al., 2017); however, concerns about the robustness of these findings remain (Sala et al., 2021; Torre & Temprado, 2022).
text.formatted: In the last decade, several meta-analyses have shown small-to-moderate positive effects of exergaming on cognitive outcomes in middle-aged and older adults (J. Y. C. <ref type="bibr">Chan et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Manser et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Soares et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Stanmore et al., 2017)</ref>; however, concerns about the robustness of these findings remain <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Sala et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Torre & Temprado, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The key issues are the substantial heterogeneity in the methods across studies and, consequently, in the results reported, as well as the potential influence of publication bias, which previous studies have not consistently or adequately addressed.
One way to address the substantial heterogeneity observed across studies is to investigate potential moderators of exergaming on cognitive outcomes.

Sample characteristics (e.g., age, clinical vs. non-clinical populations, baseline cognitive status), intervention characteristics (e.g., session duration and frequency, intervention duration), as well as type of product (commercial vs. researcher-developed exergames) and delivery mode, may systematically influence effect sizes.

Identifying such moderators is essential for clarifying the conditions under which exergaming interventions are most effective across diverse populations (Torre & Temprado, 2022). Manser et al. (2024) conducted one of the most comprehensive metaanalyses on exergames and cognition in middle-aged and older adults.
text.formatted: Identifying such moderators is essential for clarifying the conditions under which exergaming interventions are most effective across diverse populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Torre & Temprado, 2022)</ref>. <ref type="bibr">Manser et al. (2024)</ref> conducted one of the most comprehensive metaanalyses on exergames and cognition in middle-aged and older adults.

text.text: Their findings indicated that the intervention effects are not moderated by population type (clinical vs. non-clinical) or cognitive status (healthy vs. impaired).

However, they observed significant moderation effects on EFs as a function of: (i) type of motor-cognitive training, with simultaneous motor-cognitive training outperforming simultaneous-additional (dual-task) training; (ii) body position, with exergames requiring stepping proving more effective than those that require only standing; (iii) training intensity, with greater effects observed for moderate-intensity exergames.
Notably, dose-response variables such as session duration, frequency, and overall intervention length did not significantly moderate effectiveness.
Previous studies have also examined both commercial and research-developed exergames to assess their impact on physical and cognitive outcomes.
Commercial exergames, while primarily designed for entertainment, also offer opportunities for physical and cognitive interventions in motivating environments (Kappen et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Commercial exergames, while primarily designed for entertainment, also offer opportunities for physical and cognitive interventions in motivating environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Kappen et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, researcher-developed exergames are typically grounded in behavioral and cognitive science, with targeted design features intended to improve specific physical and cognitive health outcomes (Kharrazi et al., 2012; Lu & Kharrazi, 2018). Manser et al. (2024) did not observe differences in effect size between commercial and researcher-developed exergames, although previous research has suggested that exergame design should be tailored to the specific needs of diverse populations to improve clinical efficacy (Torre & Temprado, 2022).

(2024)</ref> did not observe differences in effect size between commercial and researcher-developed exergames, although previous research has suggested that exergame design should be tailored to the specific needs of diverse populations to improve clinical efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Torre & Temprado, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, over the last decade, there has been an increasing number of studies investigating the effects of virtual reality (VR) exergames on cognition with promising effects (Adcock et al., 2020; Droby et al., 2020; Grosprêtre et al., 2023; Maggio et al., 2022; Thapa et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Additionally, over the last decade, there has been an increasing number of studies investigating the effects of virtual reality (VR) exergames on cognition with promising effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adcock et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Droby et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Grosprêtre et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Maggio et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Thapa et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: VR exergames use computer-generated 3-D environments that players can explore and interact with in real time through devices such as head-mounted displays.
By combining immersive VR technology with physical activity, these games create engaging, lifelike exercise experiences that stimulate perceptual, cognitive, and motor processes.

Thus, exergames should be considered a class of interactive systems whose efficacy in shaping different aspects of cognition might depend on their design features and engagement mechanics (Deterding et al., 2011; Sailer et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Thus, exergames should be considered a class of interactive systems whose efficacy in shaping different aspects of cognition might depend on their design features and engagement mechanics <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Deterding et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Sailer et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This meta-analysis seeks to reassess the magnitude, uncertainty, and robustness of the evidence on the cognitive effects of exergames in adults aged 50 and above, based on studies published up to May 31, 2024 (K = 48).
text.formatted: This meta-analysis seeks to reassess the magnitude, uncertainty, and robustness of the evidence on the cognitive effects of exergames in adults aged 50 and above, based on studies published up to <ref type="bibr">May 31, 2024 (K = 48)</ref>.

text.text: We (i) estimate the overall and domain-specific effects of exergames on cognition; (ii) investigate key moderators of exergaming's efficacy such as intervention dose, product type (i.e., commercial vs. researcher-developed exergames), modality (i.e., screen vs.

VR-based), or intervention design features (e.g., training dose, blinding, controls); and (iii) employ a Bayesian statistical framework to better characterize variability and uncertainty in exergame effects, as well as evaluate their robustness after accounting for publication bias.
While recent meta-analyses have provided insight into the effects of exergames on cognition, only one has examined potential factors moderating their effects (Manser et al., 2024).
text.formatted: While recent meta-analyses have provided insight into the effects of exergames on cognition, only one has examined potential factors moderating their effects <ref type="bibr">(Manser et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, important methodological limitations remain, particularly regarding the handling of publication bias and the reliance on frequentist approaches.
Publication bias is an ongoing concern in meta-analytic studies that threatens the validity of the results and needs to be carefully addressed (Rothstein et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Publication bias is an ongoing concern in meta-analytic studies that threatens the validity of the results and needs to be carefully addressed <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Rothstein et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Previous meta-analyses on this topic did not detect publication bias (J. Y. C. Chan et al., 2024; Manser et al., 2024; Stanmore et al., 2017), or did not examine it (Soares et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Previous meta-analyses on this topic did not detect publication bias (J. Y. C. <ref type="bibr">Chan et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Manser et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Stanmore et al., 2017)</ref>, or did not examine it <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Soares et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, a reanalysis of studies included in Stanmore et al. (2017) detected publication bias and yielded a small to null effect of exergames on cognitive ability in older adults (Sala et al., 2021).
text.formatted: However, a reanalysis of studies included in <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Stanmore et al. (2017)</ref> detected publication bias and yielded a small to null effect of exergames on cognitive ability in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Sala et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, Chan et al. (2024) and Manser et al. (2024) examined publication bias using Egger's regression test; however, they applied the test separately to each outcome, a strategy that is known to have limited power when the number of studies is small and between-study heterogeneity is substantial (Higgins, J. P. T. et al., 2019; J. A. C. Sterne et al., 2011).

(2024)</ref> examined publication bias using Egger's regression test; however, they applied the test separately to each outcome, a strategy that is known to have limited power when the number of studies is small and between-study heterogeneity is substantial (Higgins, J. P. T. et al., 2019; J. A. C. <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Sterne et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Further, previous meta-analyses have handled the dependence between multiple outcomes from the same study inconsistently: Chan et al.

(2024) retained a single outcome measure per cognitive domain, Soares et al. (2021) analyzed each outcome measure separately, others averaged outcomes within studies without specifying the correlation between them (Manser et al., 2024; Stanmore et al., 2017), whereas only the reanalysis by Sala et al. (Sala et al., 2021) explicitly modeled dependent effect sizes, using robust variance estimation (Hedges et al., 2010).

(2021)</ref> analyzed each outcome measure separately, others averaged outcomes within studies without specifying the correlation between them <ref type="bibr">(Manser et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Stanmore et al., 2017)</ref>, whereas only the reanalysis by Sala et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Sala et al., 2021)</ref> explicitly modeled dependent effect sizes, using robust variance estimation <ref type="bibr">(Hedges et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, frequentist statistical methods emphasize decision thresholds such as p-values rather than providing a nuanced, probabilistic characterization of the evidence of effects and their respective uncertainty.
Consequently, frequentist approaches may yield significant effects, even when the strength of underlying evidence is minimal or uncertain (Moran & Linden, 2024).
text.formatted: Consequently, frequentist approaches may yield significant effects, even when the strength of underlying evidence is minimal or uncertain <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Moran & Linden, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This limitation is especially problematic in exergaming research, where both the number of available studies and their respective sample sizes remain relatively small, and their methodological heterogeneity across studies is high (Torre & Temprado, 2022).
text.formatted: This limitation is especially problematic in exergaming research, where both the number of available studies and their respective sample sizes remain relatively small, and their methodological heterogeneity across studies is high <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Torre & Temprado, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The Bayesian framework offers a flexible and informative approach to quantifying effects and their associated uncertainty.

Bayesian sampling methods generate full posterior distributions for each parameter, allowing researchers to quantify uncertainty and assess the credibility of observed effects with greater nuance (Moran & Linden, 2024; Sutton & Abrams, 2001).
text.formatted: Bayesian sampling methods generate full posterior distributions for each parameter, allowing researchers to quantify uncertainty and assess the credibility of observed effects with greater nuance <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Moran & Linden, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Sutton & Abrams, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: To address the concerns outlined above, the present study employed multilevel Robust Bayesian Model-Averaging (RoBMA) (Bartoš et al., 2026), which can be implemented regardless of the presence of publication bias.
text.formatted: To address the concerns outlined above, the present study employed multilevel Robust Bayesian Model-Averaging (RoBMA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bartoš et al., 2026)</ref>, which can be implemented regardless of the presence of publication bias.

text.text: This approach provides robust effect size estimates by accounting for publication bias, heterogeneity, and pooled effects, while also estimating the level of evidence for both the null and alternative hypotheses (Maier et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This approach provides robust effect size estimates by accounting for publication bias, heterogeneity, and pooled effects, while also estimating the level of evidence for both the null and alternative hypotheses <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Maier et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Multilevel RoBMA enables modeling dependencies arising from multiple effect sizes nested within studies and therefore, all available outcomes can be retained while estimating the between and within-study heterogeneity.
Importantly, we report pooled effects from models without publication bias adjustment, alongside RoBMA's publication bias adjusted estimates.

This integrated approach allows us to evaluate whether both the cognitive effects of exergaming and the factors hypothesized to influence those effects remain supported after jointly accounting for publication bias, between and within-study heterogeneity, and model uncertainty.
These features can make Bayesian meta-analysis not only more robust to heterogeneity and outliers, but also less dependent on any single method of bias detection (Röver et al., 2021).
text.formatted: These features can make Bayesian meta-analysis not only more robust to heterogeneity and outliers, but also less dependent on any single method of bias detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Röver et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, together these features enable a more comprehensive evaluation of both the cognitive effects of exergaming and the conditions under which those effects are most likely to emerge in adults over 50, a population at increased risk for cognitive decline with advancing age (Singh-Manoux et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Thus, together these features enable a more comprehensive evaluation of both the cognitive effects of exergaming and the conditions under which those effects are most likely to emerge in adults over 50, a population at increased risk for cognitive decline with advancing age <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">(Singh-Manoux et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Using this approach, we will build on the literature by addressing the following questions: (i) Do exergame interventions improve cognition in midlife and older adults?
(ii) Are the effects of exergaming moderated by individual factors such as age and population characteristics (e.g., non-clinical vs. clinical conditions)?
And (iii) Do product type (commercial vs. researcher-developed exergames), game modality (screen vs.
VR-based) and intervention characteristics (e.g., training frequency, session and intervention duration) moderate cognitive outcomes?

text.text: Inclusion criteria required intervention studies to be: (i) original and published in peerreviewed, English-language journals or comprehensive conference proceedings; (ii) exergame interventions must be interactive and electronically powered; (iii) exergames must involve gross motor movements rather than simple finger or handheld motions, as such activity is believed to stimulate cardiovascular and neurophysiological processes linked to cognitive benefits (Erickson et al., 2019); (iv) the exergame intervention was required to include enhancement, maintenance, or restoration of cognitive function as an intervention aim, although cognitive measures were not required to be designated as the primary outcome of the original study; (v) interventions must use exergaming technology as the sole or primary treatment modality (i.e., representing > 50% of the intervention) to ensure that exergaming was the dominant component driving potential cognitive effects; (vi) the study design must include at least two conditions (i.e., between-subjects design with at least a control group) with a minimum of 10 participants per condition, as a pragmatic lower bound to ensure a basic level of statistical stability, and reduce the influence of sampling error that could be disproportionately high in extremely small samples (Kühberger et al., 2014); (vii) the exergame intervention had a minimum training duration of one week, as the pragmatic lower bound in prior exergaming trials, intended to exclude single-session or very short-term effects that are more likely to reflect task-specific learning rather than meaningful neurocognitive change, though we recognize that in practice most studies should ideally span a longer duration; and (viii) the mean participant age must be > 50 years.

text.text: Studies employing single-group pre-/posttest or post-test-only designs were excluded.
Control conditions consisted of either traditional training/therapies or passive control groups.
Between Summer 2023 and Spring 2024, the search was conducted in two phases.
In Phase I, we searched Google Scholar and PubMed for systematic reviews and meta-analyses on exergames, active video games and VR to identify eligible primary studies.

In Phase II, we searched six international academic databases (PubMed, EBSCO [PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE], Web of Science, and Google Scholar) for primary studies published between 2016 and May 31, 2024 (see Supplemental Materials: Boolean search phrases.docx).
Together, both phases identified 6,041 potentially relevant articles published between January 1, 1996 and May 31, 2024.
A total of 534 duplicate articles were removed, and the remaining 5,507 articles were screened by three independent coders based on their abstracts.

Abstracts had to maintain sufficient information to determine that their primary aim was improving health using an exergame in adults aged 50 and above, and another 5,140 articles were excluded (See Figure 1 for details).
text.formatted: Abstracts had to maintain sufficient information to determine that their primary aim was improving health using an exergame in adults aged 50 and above, and another 5,140 articles were excluded (See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for details).

text.text: A total of 367 individual articles were selected.
Next, the coders read the full text of these articles and identified 207 articles with participants in our designated age range.
Articles were advanced in the selection process if they met all aspects of our eligibility criteria.
Further review of these articles identified 60 articles examining cognitive outcomes.
Of the 60, eight articles were excluded for lack of baseline and/or follow-up cognitive outcome data, and one study was removed during the data analysis phase since it had been retracted.
Additionally, an audit identified two cases of publications arising from overlapping participant samples.
These cases required different treatment.
In the publications by Liao et al. (2019 Liao et al. ( , 2020)), the two papers reported different cognitive outcomes from the same participant sample.

text.text: We therefore retained the non-overlapping cognitive outcomes while treating both publications as arising from a single independent study.

In contrast, two publications by Chan et al. (2023 Chan et al. ( , 2024) ) reported the same cognitive outcomes from the same underlying participant sample, and we only kept the first published study.

text.text: Finally, a re-audit of the extraction dataset led to the exclusion of a study whose outcomes were measures of postural control while performing a cognitive task (Ray et al., 2012), resulting in a total of 49 publications and 48 independent studies included in the meta-analysis.

text.text: A team of five independent coders performed data extraction.
They came from different academic backgrounds (Psychology, Biology, Public Health, Regulatory Affairs, and General Education) to provide fair and comprehensive coverage.

All coders had research experience in virtual games used for health purposes and were trained for two months in both the search and data extraction phases of coding, using 5% of the included articles.
During the preparation period (May to June 2024), all coders received two training sessions per week and coded the same 5% subset of the included articles.
The coding sheet incorporated all data extraction variables as well as the risk of bias assessment items.

Inter-rater reliability, calculated as percent agreement across coders on all outcome variables from the overlapping training articles, reached ≥ 87% on a weekly basis before the main coding phase began.
During the main coding period, the remaining articles were divided among the coders so that each article was coded by a primary coder.

To prevent single-coder error, every coded article was then independently checked against the original source for coding accuracy and completeness by two additional coders (from the same team of five), who flagged and corrected any discrepancies, with inter-rater reliability monitored continuously throughout the coding period.
We conducted two formal calibration exercises (mid-point and end of the coding period), in which inter-rater reliability was ≥ 92%.
This single-coder-extraction-with-twoindependent-verification protocol is an accepted alternative to full duplicate extraction (Büchter et al., 2020; Garritty et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This single-coder-extraction-with-twoindependent-verification protocol is an accepted alternative to full duplicate extraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Büchter et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Garritty et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Using a standardized data extraction sheet, information about the characteristics of each study was retrieved, including: (i) study characteristics (i.e. author, year of publication, country, sample size, blindness statement, environment), (ii) population characteristics (i.e., non-clinical vs. clinical conditions such as ADRD, Parkinson's disease, stroke patients, etc.) and demographics (i.e., age and sex), (iii) exergame features, such as platform/modality (e.g., console, VR-system, computer-based, etc.), and type of product (i.e., commercial vs. researcher-developed exergames), (iv) specific names of the outcome measures used in each study, as well as the cognitive constructs they intended to measure, and (v) intervention characteristics: single session duration, intervention frequency (i.e., days/week) and intervention duration (i.e., number of weeks).
Authors were contacted using a standardized email template when their publications did not contain all the information listed above.
In total, the 48 included studies provided 181 effects on diverse cognitive outcomes.
These were initially classified into 15 cognitive domains.
To ensure an adequate number of effect sizes within each category, conceptually related domains were subsequently combined prior to analysis, resulting in 11 cognitive domains.

Specifically, task outcomes such as inhibitory control, sustained attention and divided attention were combined into a single attentional control domain, general executive function was incorporated into global cognition, and verbal fluency and language processing were combined into a single language domain.
The initial classification was performed by a senior researcher (AFK), a co-author with over 40 years of expertise in cognition, and independently verified by two additional coders (MYE and QC).
Agreement was near perfect (Krippendorff's α = 0.983 for nominal data) measured through Krippendorff's test (Marzi et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Agreement was near perfect (Krippendorff's α = 0.983 for nominal data) measured through Krippendorff's test <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Marzi et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The few discrepancies were resolved by consensus.
The main analysis examined the overall effect of exergames across cognitive outcomes and their potential moderators.
Due to the limited data available in some of these outcomes, we limited our analyses to the five cognitive domains for which at least data from

To assess the risk of bias of the included articles, the classic Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 1.0) was applied (Higgins et al., 2011).
text.formatted: To assess the risk of bias of the included articles, the classic Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 1.0) was applied <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Higgins et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The six RoB 1.0 domains included (i) random assignment (to avoid selection bias), (ii) allocation concealment (to further avoid selection bias), (iii) blinding of participants and personnel (to avoid performance bias), (iv) blinding of outcome assessment (to avoid detection bias), (v) completeness of reporting of some outcome data (to avoid attrition bias), and (vi) selectivity in reporting (to avoid reporting bias).
We added a seventh criterion, which assessed whether there was any potential bias due to any confounding variables noted during data extraction.
Each category was given a score from -1 to +1, where -1 represented high risk of bias, 0 represented unclear risk, and 1 represented low risk of bias.
The overall score was an average of each individual component on the -1 to +1 scale.
None of the articles were excluded based on their risk-of-bias assessment.

To examine whether exergaming impacts cognition, change scores were computed (i.e., post-test minus baseline score for intervention and control groups, respectively) on each of the effects reported across each included study.

In cases in which studies did not report the standard deviations (SD) of the change scores, these were calculated from the reported data using the statistical methods described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Review of Interventions (Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, 2008).
text.formatted: In cases in which studies did not report the standard deviations (SD) of the change scores, these were calculated from the reported data using the statistical methods described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Review of Interventions (Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of <ref type="bibr">Interventions, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the SD of the change scores were computed by assuming a correlation coefficient of 0.5 between baseline and post-test measures, as recommended (Morris & DeShon, 2002).
text.formatted: Thus, the SD of the change scores were computed by assuming a correlation coefficient of 0.5 between baseline and post-test measures, as recommended <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Morris & DeShon, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Multi-arm studies were handled as follows: (i) if a study included several exergame arms and one group control (Zak et al., 2022), the exergame arms were combined into a single group following the Cochrane Handbook (Higgins, J. P. T. et al., 2019); (ii) if a study included one exergame arm and two group control arms of the same type (Karssemeijer et al., 2019; M. Park & Ha, 2023), the group control arms were combined in the same way; and (iii) if the same exergame group was compared with both a passive and an active or alternative control groups (Hou et al., 2023; Sturnieks et al., 2024), both comparisons were retained and the sample size of the exergame group was divided between them to avoid double-counting participants.

text.text: Next, standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) were calculated for the pre-post differences between intervention and control groups for each of the 181 effects included, with values of approximately 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 conventionally interpreted as small, medium, and large effect size, respectively (Cohen, 1988).

text.text: To test the overall effect of exergames on cognition (i.e., overall effect across 181 effect sizes from a diverse set of cognitive outcomes), we employed a Bayesian multilevel model with effect sizes nested within independent studies (Bartoš et al., 2026).
text.formatted: To test the overall effect of exergames on cognition (i.e., overall effect across 181 effect sizes from a diverse set of cognitive outcomes), we employed a Bayesian multilevel model with effect sizes nested within independent studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bartoš et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: At the first level, the observed effect size 𝑦 𝑖𝑗 (effect 𝑖 in study 𝑗) is treated as an estimate of its true effect 𝜃 𝑖𝑗 : with 𝜎 𝑖𝑗 2 representing the sampling variance.
At the second level, true effects within a study vary around the study mean:
At the third level, study means vary around the overall effect: with 𝜇 representing the overall pooled effect, and 𝜏 𝑏𝑒𝑡𝑤𝑒𝑒𝑛 2 and 𝜏 𝑤𝑖𝑡ℎ𝑖𝑛 2 the between-and within-study heterogeneity.

Subgroup analyses were conducted to examine the impact of exergames on cognitive domains for which data from at least 10 independent studies was available (i.e., global cognition, processing speed, cognitive flexibility, attentional control and working memory).
Additionally, Bayesian multilevel meta-regression models were conducted to explore potential moderators impacting exergames on cognition.

We examined the following moderators: (i) age, (ii) population (non-clinical vs. clinical condition), (iii) duration of individual intervention sessions, (iv) frequency of intervention sessions, (v) total intervention length, (vi) training modality (i.e., screen-based vs.
VR-based exergames), (vii) product type (commercially available exergames vs. games developed by research teams), (viii) blinding type, (ix) group control type, and (x) risk of bias.

We fitted several meta-regression models by moderator set: (i) age, (ii) population, (iii) control type, (iv) session duration, session frequency and intervention duration, (v) exergame training modality and product type, (vi) blinding and (vii) risk of bias.
Heterogeneity across studies was evaluated by examining the posterior distributions of the between and within-study heterogeneity parameter (between, within).
Publication bias was assessed by visually inspecting funnel plots of standard errors and the use of Egger's test (Egger et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Publication bias was assessed by visually inspecting funnel plots of standard errors and the use of Egger's test <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Egger et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Further, multilevel NoBMA (i.e., Bayesian meta-analytic models without publication-bias adjustment) and multilevel RoBMA models were employed.

In this framework, NoBMA provides pooled (and moderator) estimates under multilevel random-effects models, whereas RoBMA additionally accounts for publication bias and model uncertainty by averaging across a set of candidate models that vary in whether they assume (i) the presence vs. absence of publication bias; (ii) the presence vs. absence of heterogeneity, and (iii) a non-zero vs. null effect.

We used a normally distributed small positive effect prior for the pooled effect (𝑁(0.30, 0.15)), based on previous meta-analytic evidence (Manser et al., 2024), against a point null hypothesis (μ = 0).
text.formatted: We used a normally distributed small positive effect prior for the pooled effect (𝑁(0.30, 0.15)), based on previous meta-analytic evidence <ref type="bibr">(Manser et al., 2024)</ref>, against a point null hypothesis (μ = 0).

text.text: Heterogeneity was assigned a N(0.30, 0.20) prior truncated at zero.
For the meta-regression model, we included a prior for the moderators' effect N(0.05, 0.15) along the prior described above for the primary overall effect.
All analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024).
The brms R package was used to fit the Bayesian hierarchical Egger's model (Bürkner, 2017), whereas the RoBMA R package was used to fit hierarchical NoBMA and RoBMA models (Maier et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The brms R package was used to fit the Bayesian hierarchical Egger's model <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bürkner, 2017)</ref>, whereas the RoBMA R package was used to fit hierarchical NoBMA and RoBMA models <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Maier et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Posterior distributions for all models were sampled using Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling (MCMC) with 5 chains, each comprising 100,000 iterations.
Bayes factors (BF) were used to quantify the relative evidence provided by the data for the alternative hypothesis (H1) versus the null hypothesis (H0) of an exactly zero effect (μ = 0).
BF were interpreted as continuous measures of relative evidence.
For interpretability, we report conventional benchmarks based on Jeffreys' BF evidence scale (Jeffreys, H., 1998; Wagenmakers et al., 2010).
text.formatted: For interpretability, we report conventional benchmarks based on Jeffreys' BF evidence scale (Jeffreys, H., 1998; <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Wagenmakers et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: BF10 between 1 and 3 indicates anecdotal evidence for the H1, 3-10 moderate evidence, 10-30 strong evidence, 30-100 very strong evidence, and >100 decisive evidence for H1.
text.formatted: BF10 between 1 and 3 indicates anecdotal evidence for the H1, 3-10 moderate evidence, 10-30 strong evidence, 30-100 very strong evidence, and >100 decisive evidence for H1.

text.text: BF₁₀ values below 1 indicate evidence for the H0, interpreted with the reciprocal thresholds: 1/3-1 anecdotal, 1/10-1/3 moderate, 1/30-1/10 strong, 1/100-1/30 very strong, and < 1/100 decisive evidence for H0.

text.text: We refer to anecdotal evidence in either direction (1/3 < BF₁₀ < 3) as inconclusive.

text.text: A systematic search yielded 6,041 potentially relevant articles, of which 367 remained after removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts.
Following the initial screening, 207 articles were retained after the full-text review.
Based on the predefined eligibility criteria, 49 articles from 48 independent intervention studies published between 2010 and 2024 were included in the meta-analysis.
The included studies comprised 181 effects across diverse cognitive outcomes.
Details of the study characteristics are presented in Supplemental Materials (Table S1).

The average proportion of male participants across studies was 38.69%.

text.text: Geographically, the 48 studies were conducted across five regions: Asia (k = 26), Europe (k = 15), Oceania (k = 3), North America (k = 2), and South America (k = 2).
Exergaming interventions varied widely in duration, frequency, and overall length.
Session durations ranged from 15 to 100 minutes (M = 45.52, SD = 20.50): fewer than 30 minutes (k = 8), 30-45 minutes (k = 20), and more than 45 minutes (k = 20).
Training frequency ranged from 1 to ), and 5 days/week (k = 4).
Intervention durations spanned 3 to 26 weeks (M = 10.45, SD = 6.01).
Regarding exergaming platforms, 30 studies employed screen-based gaming consoles, while 18 studies used VR-based systems.
Among the screen-based interventions, the Nintendo Wii or Wii U (k = 10) and Microsoft Xbox Kinect (k = 10) were the most frequently used, followed by dance pad or dance platform systems (k = 5).
Of the VR-based systems, 5 studies used fully immersive headsets, while the remaining 13 utilized room-scale VR installations.
Most studies (k = 30) used commercially available exergames.
The remaining 18 studies used researcherdeveloped exergames tailored to specific intervention goals.
Most studies (k = 41) did not require an internet connection to play.
Exergames were also coded for narrative integration as a motivational design feature (Lu, 2015).
text.formatted: Exergames were also coded for narrative integration as a motivational design feature <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Lu, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Only one game, Nintendo Ring Fit Adventure, included some narrative components.
In terms of setting, 25 studies were conducted in field environments, including 13 in hospitals, 6 in group living facilities, 3 in home environments, and 3 in physical therapy practices.
Further, 9 studies were conducted in laboratory settings, and 3 studies did not specify a setting.
The remaining 11 studies were conducted across multiple or alternative settings.
Most studies compared exergaming against an alternative treatment control condition (k = 28).
Note that all these studies included populations with clinical conditions.
Additionally, a smaller proportion of studies used active control groups (k = 9) or only a passive control (k = 9).
The remaining two studies included two control groups: an alternative treatment and a passive control group (Hou et al., 2023), and an active and a passive control group (Sturnieks et al., 2024).

text.text: Overall, the mean risk-ofbias score was 0.44 (SD = 0.40; range: -0.43 to 1.00).
The most common high-risk factor was the lack of blinding of participants and personnel, observed in 58% of studies.
Additionally, 33% of studies demonstrated risk of bias due to lack of blinding in outcome assessment, and approximately 27% showed risk of bias due to inadequate allocation concealment.

In contrast, the most frequently observed indicators of a low risk of bias were complete reporting of outcome data (98%), use of random assignment (83%), avoidance of selective reporting (75%), and efforts to minimize other sources of bias (75%).
A total of 181 effect sizes were extracted, each representing a cognitive measure.
These outcomes were initially categorized into 15 cognitive domains and subsequently consolidated into 11 cognitive domains as explained above (see Methods).
Because some studies contributed with multiple outcomes, the total sample size in each domain exceeds the total sample size due to within-study multiplicity.

The 11 cognitive domains included: global cognition (k = 29; n = 1,584), processing speed (k = 23; n = 1,163), cognitive flexibility (k = 22; n = 1,544), attentional control (k = 16; n = 916), working memory (k = 14; n = 897), short-term memory (k = 8; n = 569), longterm memory (k = 7; n = 261), visuospatial processing (k = 6; n = 249), motor control (k = 3; n = 154), language (k = 4; n = 423), and episodic memory (k = 2; n = 154).

We use the term "global cognition" to refer to screening measures for older adults' global cognitive functioning, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) (Nasreddine et al., 2005) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) (Folstein et al., 1983).

text.text: First, we evaluated the overall impact of exergames on cognition using a Bayesian multilevel meta-analytic model.

This model pooled 181 effect sizes across all cognitive domains, enabling estimation of a study-level average effect while accounting for intra-study dependency due to multiple cognitive outcomes reported within the same study.
The meta-analysis revealed that the standardized mean difference (SMD) was 0.31 (BF10 > 1000) suggesting a small positive effect of exergames across cognitive outcomes (K = 48).
text.formatted: The meta-analysis revealed that the standardized mean difference (SMD) was 0.31 (BF10 > 1000) suggesting a small positive effect of exergames across cognitive outcomes (K = 48).

text.text: The total heterogeneity was 0.25 (95% CrI = [0.17, 0.34]; BF10 > 1000), indicating decisive evidence for moderate variability in effect sizes across studies.
text.formatted: The total heterogeneity was 0.25 (95% CrI = [0.17, 0.34]; BF10 > 1000), indicating decisive evidence for moderate variability in effect sizes across studies.

text.text: To evaluate the potential impact of publication bias on the overall effect across cognitive outcomes, we examined a funnel plot and conducted the Egger's regression test.
Figure 3 shows the funnel plot of observed effect sizes against their standard errors, where visual inspection suggests funnel-plot asymmetry.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref> shows the funnel plot of observed effect sizes against their standard errors, where visual inspection suggests funnel-plot asymmetry.

text.text: Specifically, there is a skew toward studies reporting positive effects of exergames on cognition.
Individual effect sizes and their 95% confidence intervals are shown in the forest plot in the Supplemental Materials (forest_plot_all_outcomes.pdf).
Egger's regression analysis did not provide strong support for the visual impression of publication bias (estimate = 0.14; 95% CrI = [-0.24, 0.51]; BF10 = 1.25).
The estimated effect after accounting for small-study effects in the Egger regression was SMD = 0.27 (95% CrI = [0.13, 0.42]; BF10 = 68.98).

On the other hand, after accounting for publication bias using the multilevel RoBMA framework, the estimated SMD was 0.13 (BF10 = 1.05), and the publication bias inclusion factor provided anecdotal evidence for publication bias (BF10 = 2.39) in line with Egger's regression test.
Multilevel RoBMA yielded a smaller adjusted estimate than the Egger regression, and the evidence for an overall effect after adjusting for publication bias was inconclusive.

text.text: For global cognition, a small effect (SMD = 0.37, BF10 > 1000) was observed accompanied by substantial between-study heterogeneity (τ = 0.39; 95% CrI = [0.25, 0.56]; BF10 > 1000).
text.formatted: For global cognition, a small effect (SMD = 0.37, BF10 > 1000) was observed accompanied by substantial between-study heterogeneity (τ = 0.39; 95% CrI = [0.25, 0.56]; BF10 > 1000).

text.text: A small effect was found for processing speed (SMD = 0.28, BF10 = 52.25) with moderate between-study heterogeneity (τ = 0.28; 95% CrI = [0.00, 0.47]; BF10 = 26.32).
For cognitive flexibility, a small effect was also observed (SMD = 0.21, BF10 = 13.04) with moderate heterogeneity (τ = 0.23; 95% CrI = [0, 0.42]; BF10 = 9.04).
A small effect was detected for attentional control (SMD = 0.23, BF10 = 356.91) with very low heterogeneity (τ = 0.01; 95% CrI = [0.00, 0.16]; BF10 = 0.15).
Finally, working memory showed a small effect (SMD = 0.21, BF10 = 12.62) with low heterogeneity (τ = 0.07; 95% CrI = [0.00, 0.38]; BF10 = 0.55).

After accounting for publication bias (multilevel RoBMA), there was anecdotal evidence for a small positive effect of exergaming on global cognition, and substantial uncertainty around the magnitude of the effect (SMD = 0.23, 95% CrI = [0.00, 0.49]; BF10 = 2.47).
There was anecdotal evidence for effects on processing speed (SMD = 0.14, BF10 = 1.35).
There was anecdotal evidence favoring the null hypothesis for cognitive flexibility (SMD = 0.08, BF10 = 0.63).
There was anecdotal evidence for a positive effect on attentional control (SMD = 0.11, BF10 = 1.32).
For working memory, the data favored the null hypothesis after accounting for publication bias (SMD = 0.04, BF10 = 0.33).
Importantly, the evidence for publication bias varied across cognitive domains.

There was anecdotal evidence favoring publication bias models for global cognition (BF10 bias = 1.18), processing speed (BF10 bias = 1.61), attentional control (BF10 bias = 1.68) and cognitive flexibility (BF10 bias = 2.49), with the strongest evidence for publication bias observed for working memory (BF10 bias = 10.08).
There was no evidence that mean age or population condition moderated the effect of exergaming on cognition, with inclusion Bayes factors below 1 in both NoBMA and RoBMA models.
Thus, the data favored models excluding these participant-level characteristics as moderators.
There was little evidence that intervention dosage moderated the effects of exergaming on cognition.
Session duration and session frequency showed inclusion Bayes factors below 1 in both NoBMA and RoBMA models, favoring models excluding these factors.

Intervention duration yielded only anecdotal evidence for inclusion before and after accounting for model uncertainty and publication bias (NoBMA BF10 = 2.62; RoBMA BF10 = 1.25), with slightly smaller estimates for interventions with longer duration.
There was no evidence that exergame modality (VR-based vs. screen-based exergames) moderated intervention effects, with inclusion Bayes factors below 1 in both NoBMA and RoBMA models.
Similarly, product type (commercially available vs. researcher-developed exergames) showed no evidence for moderation (NoBMA BF10 = 0.44; RoBMA BF10 = 0.42).
Among the methodological factors examined, the evidence did not support the inclusion of control type as moderating factor (NoBMA BF10 = 0.18; RoBMA BF10 = 0.16).
Blinding showed no evidence for moderator inclusion, indicating limited evidence that intervention effects differed according to blinding status (NoBMA BF10 = 0.30; RoBMA BF10 = 0.25).
Further, risk of bias showed no evidence for moderator inclusion in either modeling approach (NoBMA BF10 = 0.29; RoBMA BF10 = 0.29).

Overall, these findings suggest that, after accounting for heterogeneity, model uncertainty, and publication bias, individual-level and methodological factors did not show evidence supporting their role as moderators.
These exploratory findings should be confirmed in future meta-analyses with a larger evidence base, which would increase statistical power to detect moderator effects.
We evaluated the sensitivity of the findings to alternative prior specifications.

For the overall effect and the cognitive domains, we tested alternative effect priors [N(0, 0.25), N(0.30, 0.30), and N(0, 1)] relative to the primary N(0.30, 0.15) prior, as well as the RoBMA default prior for heterogeneity.
For the meta-regression, we retained the primary prior for the overall effect and tested a zero-centered prior [N(0, 0.15)] for moderator effects relative to the primary N(0.05, 0.15) specification.

After adjusting for publication bias, the evidence for an overall effect remained inconclusive under the N(0, 0.25) and N(0.30, 0.30) priors (BF₁₀ = 0.74 and 0.70 respectively) and under the default heterogeneity prior (BF₁₀ = 1.02), and it favored the null hypothesis under the wider N(0, 1) default RoBMA prior (BF₁₀ = 0.29).
No moderator showed evidence for inclusion under the alternative moderator prior (RoBMA BF₁₀ ≤ 1.67).
We also examined the sensitivity of the overall findings to alternative assumed pre-post correlations (r = 0.20 and 0.80, relative to r = 0.50 in the primary analysis).

As expected, the assumed correlation affected effect-size magnitude and evidence strength (RoBMA: SMD = 0.17, BF₁₀ = 2.77 and SMD = 0.00, BF₁₀ = 0.10, respectively), but the evidence did not support a robust overall effect under either assumption.
As an additional sensitivity analysis, we repeated the analyses after excluding studies that did not use fully randomized allocation procedures (k = 41; 167 effect sizes).

The overall effect was slightly attenuated (NoBMA: SMD = 0.28; BF10 > 1000; RoBMA: SMD = 0.11; BF10 = 0.93), the evidence for publication bias remained anecdotal (BF₁₀ = 2.30), and no cognitive domain showed more than anecdotal evidence for an effect.

text.text: The evidence for an overall effect also remained inconclusive when excluding effect sizes whose standard deviations were derived from standard errors, interquartile ranges or ranges (BF10 = 0.95) and when excluding studies at high risk of bias in random sequence generation, allocation concealment or outcome-assessor blinding (BF₁₀ = 0.85, 1.23 and 0.83, respectively), and it ranged from BF₁₀ = 0.46 to 3.43 when each study was left out (leave-one-out analysis).

To address the dependence between sampling errors of outcomes measured in the same participants, we also aggregated effect sizes within studies assuming within-study correlations of r = 0.30, 0.50 and 0.70 (Borenstein et al., 2009).
text.formatted: To address the dependence between sampling errors of outcomes measured in the same participants, we also aggregated effect sizes within studies assuming within-study correlations of r = 0.30, 0.50 and 0.70 <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Borenstein et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The evidence for an overall effect remained inconclusive (RoBMA BF₁₀ = 2.50, 1.77 and 1.64, respectively), and only processing speed showed moderate evidence for an effect in two of these aggregated models (BF₁₀ = 3.59, BF₁₀ = 3.36; r = 0.30, 0.50 and 0.70 respectively).
Convergence was considered as satisfactory in the models fitted for the main analysis.
The leave-one-study-out refits were run with lighter MCMC settings and were not included in the convergence diagnostics.
In total, the sensitivity analyses comprised 160 additional models (including 48 leave-one-study-out refits).
A full report of the sensitivity analysis conducted, and the convergence diagnostics of the models tested, can be found in Supplemental Materials (Sensitivity_Outputs_Report.html).
This meta-analysis reassessed the magnitude, uncertainty, and robustness of the evidence on the cognitive effects of exergames in adults aged 50 and above published up to May 31, 2024.
To do it, we employed Bayesian meta-analytic techniques which allow to quantify the uncertainty and robustness of the effects (Moran & Linden, 2024; Röver et al., 2021).
text.formatted: To do it, we employed Bayesian meta-analytic techniques which allow to quantify the uncertainty and robustness of the effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Moran & Linden, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Röver et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, we investigated the impact on cognitive outcomes of exergaming interventions among adults aged 50 and above, guided by three primary questions: (i) Do exergame interventions improve cognition in this population?
(ii) Are the effects moderated by individual factors?
and (iii) Are the effects moderated by methodological factors related to the intervention?
This study extends previous work by offering a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous synthesis of exergames' cognitive effects in middle-aged and older adults.

Several aspects of the present findings warrant further discussion, particularly regarding methodological limitations observed in prior research and the implications for future implementations of exergames as cognitive interventions for middle-aged and older adults.
Do exergame interventions improve cognitive outcomes?
text.formatted: <head>Do exergame interventions improve cognitive outcomes?
</head>

text.text: Without adjustment for publication bias our findings support a small positive effect of exergames on cognition.
However, after accounting for publication bias, heterogeneity, and model uncertainty, the estimated effect was attenuated and the evidence was inconclusive.

The evidence for publication bias was anecdotal though and therefore, the adjusted estimate should be understood as an average across models with and without publication bias weighted by their posterior probabilities.
This result is consistent with previous findings where effects became largely attenuated after accounting for publication bias (Sala et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This result is consistent with previous findings where effects became largely attenuated after accounting for publication bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Sala et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In their commentary on Stanmore et al. (2017), Sala et al. (2021) concluded that the apparent benefits of exergames become negligible after bias correction, based primarily on trim-and-fill and PET-PEESE adjustments.
text.formatted: In their commentary on <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Stanmore et al. (2017)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Sala et al. (2021)</ref> concluded that the apparent benefits of exergames become negligible after bias correction, based primarily on trim-and-fill and PET-PEESE adjustments.

text.text: RoBMA treats publication bias as a model uncertainty problem by estimating an ensemble of models that vary in whether publication bias, heterogeneity, and non-zero effects are present, relying on model-averaging inferences.
This framework reduces dependence on any single correction method chosen and explicitly propagates the uncertainty about the bias process into the pooled estimate (Maier et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This framework reduces dependence on any single correction method chosen and explicitly propagates the uncertainty about the bias process into the pooled estimate <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Maier et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The analyses by cognitive domain mirrored the overall effect.
That is, the positive estimates across all five domains were attenuated once publication bias was taken into account, leaving no cognitive domain with more than anecdotal evidence for an effect.

The evidence was anecdotal for global cognition which here referred to cognition screening measures such as the MoCA (Nasreddine et al., 2005) or the MMSE (Folstein et al., 1983), processing speed and attentional control.
text.formatted: The evidence was anecdotal for global cognition which here referred to cognition screening measures such as the MoCA <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Nasreddine et al., 2005)</ref> or the MMSE <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Folstein et al., 1983)</ref>, processing speed and attentional control.

text.text: The evidence was inconclusive for cognitive flexibility and favored the null hypothesis for working memory, the domain with the strongest evidence of publication bias.
From a game design perspective, the anecdotal evidence for domain-specific effects on cognition might still be informative.

The small and anecdotal effects observed may reflect the real-time cognitive and motor-control demands inherent in exergame play, where players must continuously select taskrelevant information, manage interference, and adjust quickly their actions in response to rapid changing in-game demands (Maggio et al., 2025; Olyaei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Wollesen et al., 2020).

text.text: We acknowledge that although this finding suggests a degree of domain specificity, caution is warranted for several reasons.
Numerical differences in the strength of evidence across domains do not establish that exergames affect some domains more than others, as these differences were not directly tested.

Moreover, core EFs, such as attentional control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory, are highly interrelated, depend on overlapping brain networks, and are often measured with tasks that are not process-pure (Friedman & Miyake, 2017; Miyake et al., 2000; Niendam et al., 2012).
