text.text: As such, isolating domain-specific effects is inherently difficult.
Furthermore, task variability across studies likely contributes to the high heterogeneity observed in these outcomes (see Supplemental Materials, Table S2).
text.formatted: Furthermore, task variability across studies likely contributes to the high heterogeneity observed in these outcomes (see Supplemental Materials, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref>).

text.text: Thus, whether specific design features, such as the real-time attentional and motor-control demands of exergame play or adaptive difficulty, can produce domain-specific benefits remains an hypothesis for future trials (Grosprêtre et al., 2023; Wollesen et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Thus, whether specific design features, such as the real-time attentional and motor-control demands of exergame play or adaptive difficulty, can produce domain-specific benefits remains an hypothesis for future trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Grosprêtre et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">Wollesen et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Do individual factors moderate exergame intervention effectiveness?
text.formatted: <head>Do individual factors moderate exergame intervention effectiveness?
</head>

text.text: One of the main goals of the present study was to examine whether the efficacy of exergaming interventions varies as a function of participants' age and population characteristics, given the substantial heterogeneity observed across the literature.

Exergaming interventions have been investigated in adults aged 50 and above across both non-clinical and clinical samples, including people with mild cognitive impairment and ADRD, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, stroke, and limited mobility.

Despite the diverse sample included in the present work, the metaregression provided evidence against moderation of the overall effect by age or population clinical condition in line with Manser et al. (2024).
text.formatted: Despite the diverse sample included in the present work, the metaregression provided evidence against moderation of the overall effect by age or population clinical condition in line with <ref type="bibr">Manser et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: These results suggest that, with the current evidence, the effects of exergames on cognition do not seem to differ substantially across age groups or between clinical and non-clinical populations.

However, given the limited number of studies per subgroup and the substantial heterogeneity within them, these analyses should be considered exploratory and therefore, differences of smaller magnitude cannot be ruled out.
Do methodological and intervention design factors moderate the impact of exergames on cognition?
text.formatted: <head>Do methodological and intervention design factors moderate the impact of exergames on cognition?
</head>

text.text: Our results revealed no conclusive evidence for a dose-response relationship between exergaming and cognitive improvement in adults aged 50 and above.
These results are consistent with Manser et al. (2024), who found limited evidence for dose-response effects of exergame interventions and their impact on cognitive functioning.
text.formatted: These results are consistent with <ref type="bibr">Manser et al. (2024)</ref>, who found limited evidence for dose-response effects of exergame interventions and their impact on cognitive functioning.

text.text: Several factors may explain the lack of moderating effects concerning dose-response intervention characteristics.

The moderators such as "session duration", "session frequency", and "total intervention duration" were characterized by imbalanced distributions across levels, which, along with high heterogeneity, likely undermined the statistical power and the likelihood of observing a moderation effect (Hempel et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The moderators such as "session duration", "session frequency", and "total intervention duration" were characterized by imbalanced distributions across levels, which, along with high heterogeneity, likely undermined the statistical power and the likelihood of observing a moderation effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Hempel et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Further, intervention duration showed a small negative association with effect size, with only anecdotal evidence for its inclusion, raising the possibility that cognitive benefits may not increase with longer training.
Whether cognitive benefits plateau or diminish with extended training due to fatigue, reduced engagement, or compliance issues should be directly examined in future studies.
Importantly, none of the 48 included studies explicitly tested dose-response hypotheses.

Thus, this meta-analysis highlights the critical need for targeted randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that systematically manipulate intervention dose to determine optimal configuration for supporting cognitive health in aging adults, in line with prior recommendations (Manser et al., 2024; Torre & Temprado, 2022).
text.formatted: Thus, this meta-analysis highlights the critical need for targeted randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that systematically manipulate intervention dose to determine optimal configuration for supporting cognitive health in aging adults, in line with prior recommendations <ref type="bibr">(Manser et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Torre & Temprado, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: There was no evidence that exergame modality (VR-based vs. screen-based) or product type (researcher-developed vs. commercially available) moderated the effects of exergames on cognition.
In both cases, the evidence was inconclusive after accounting for publication bias.
It likely reflects the imbalanced distribution of exergame types used, with most studies using commercial, screen-based exergames, as well as the residual heterogeneity across studies.

Since exergame modality only contrasted screen-based with VR-based systems, finer-grained distinctions such as between platform generations or specific design features (e.g., immersion, adaptive difficulty), could not be tested and remain open questions.

Researcher-developed exergames allow greater targeting of specific cognitive processes through tailored design (Seitz et al., 2023), and emerging interventions, such as Brain-IT, which combines multidomain exergaming with heart-rate variability biofeedback (Manser & de Bruin, 2024), illustrate this potential.
text.formatted: Researcher-developed exergames allow greater targeting of specific cognitive processes through tailored design <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">(Seitz et al., 2023)</ref>, and emerging interventions, such as Brain-IT, which combines multidomain exergaming with heart-rate variability biofeedback <ref type="bibr">(Manser & de Bruin, 2024)</ref>, illustrate this potential.

text.text: Yet, such benefits were not established by the present analyses.

By contrast, commercial titles are typically optimized primarily for entertainment and retention purposes rather than for a particular cognitive outcome (Sailer et al., 2017), which has also been suggested to be critical for improving their clinical effectiveness (Torre & Temprado, 2022).

text.text: Future trials should directly compare exergame modalities and design features to determine how they influence cognitive outcomes.
This meta-analysis is not exempt from limitations.

Each article was extracted by a welltrained primary coder, and then independently verified against the source by two additional coders with continuous inter-rater reliability monitoring, as well as full-group consensus resolution.

This single-extraction-with-independent-verification model is not equivalent to fully independent, blinded duplicate extraction, which remains the gold standard in systematic reviews (Higgins, J. P. T. et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This single-extraction-with-independent-verification model is not equivalent to fully independent, blinded duplicate extraction, which remains the gold standard in systematic reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Higgins, J. P. T. et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Because the additional coders verified the primary coders' extraction rather than extracting the data independently, some anchoring to the initial coding cannot be excluded.
Nevertheless, the use of standardized extraction forms, extensive coder training, independent

This manuscript is a preprint verification against the source, continuous monitoring of inter-rater reliability, and consensus resolution of discrepancies provided multiple safeguards to minimize extraction errors (Büchter et al., 2020; Garritty et al., 2021).

text.text: Another limitation of this meta-analysis is that only published studies in English were included, in accordance with the pre-registered PROSPERO protocol (ID: CRD42020204191).
While this approach ensured methodological consistency and transparency, it may have excluded relevant unpublished or non-English studies.
Future reviews could expand the search to include grey literature and studies published in other languages to provide a more comprehensive synthesis of global evidence.
The inclusion of studies where exergaming comprised >50% of the intervention is another limitation.
text.formatted: The inclusion of studies where exergaming comprised >50% of the intervention is another limitation.

text.text: While this threshold ensured that exergaming was the dominant component and reflected real-world practice, the choice may introduce confounds, as some cognitive benefits could also be attributed to non-exergame components.
As such, efficacy claims specific to exergaming should be interpreted cautiously, and this approach may reduce comparability with prior reviews that applied stricter inclusion criteria.
Moreover, seven of the included studies used pseudo-randomized rather than fully randomized allocation procedures.

Although these studies met the predefined eligibility criteria for controlled intervention designs, the absence of full randomization may increase susceptibility to selection bias and limit the strength of causal inference from this work.
Nevertheless, sensitivity analyses restricted to fully randomized studies largely preserved the pattern of findings, although effect estimates and Bayesian evidence were generally attenuated.

A further statistical limitation is that although the multilevel models accounted for the clustering of effect sizes within studies, they did not directly model the sampling covariance among effect sizes derived from the same participants.

However, aggregating effect sizes within studies under plausible within-study correlations led to similar conclusions, except for processing speed which showed moderate evidence for an effect only in the aggregated models.
Additionally, this meta-analysis was limited in its ability to examine differential effects on all cognitive outcomes due to the large variability of measures across studies.
Further, although this meta-analysis included a relatively large number of studies, the evidence base remained insufficient to examine interactions among moderators.
Another limitation is that the coverage of studies published before 2016 depends on the reviews identified
Several directions for future research emerge from our findings and from the methodological limitations of the existing literature.
The current evidence is based mostly on studies with small samples and limited statistical power.
While typical in emerging research areas, such limitations restrict the generalizability of meta-analytic findings and hinder the exploration of potential moderators.

Thus, large-scale, wellpowered RCTs preregistered trials are needed to clarify for whom, and under which conditions, exergaming might yield cognitive benefits (Jaeggi et al., 2014; Parong et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Thus, large-scale, wellpowered RCTs preregistered trials are needed to clarify for whom, and under which conditions, exergaming might yield cognitive benefits <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Jaeggi et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Parong et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We observed considerable variability in how EFs were assessed and operationalized.

To enhance comparability across studies, future research would benefit from (i) the adoption of standardized cognitive assessment batteries, such as the National Institute of Health (NIH) toolbox for Neurological and Behavioral Function Cognition Battery (NIH Toolbox CB) (Gershon et al., 2013), as well as from (ii) operationalizing EFs through joint measures of speed-accuracy (for a review see : Liesefeld & Janczyk, 2019; Yangüez et al., 2024) or parameters derived from diffusion models (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008).

text.text: The latter is particularly relevant in research including older adults, who tend to prioritize accuracy over speed (Starns & Ratcliff, 2012), so changes in either measure alone may reflect shifts in response strategy rather than genuine improvements in cognitive function.

text.text: Blinding remains a key methodological issue in the literature, not only in exergame interventions but in gamified cognitive and physical interventions more broadly (Kletzel et al., 2021; Pacheco et al., 2020).

text.text: Future studies should aim for blinded outcome assessment when feasible, for instance, blinding evaluators to participants' group assignments or leveraging selfadministered digital platforms to minimize bias (Öhman et al., 2021).

text.text: Another plausible mechanism is improvement in cardiovascular fitness which has been linked to cognitive enhancement and neuroplasticity in prior research (Kramer & Colcombe, 2018; Voss et al., 2016).

text.text: During the literature review conducted, however, only seven of the 48 studies included measured cardiovascular fitness as one of their outcomes.
While we acknowledge that it is not feasible to include in every intervention a gold-standard measure of cardiovascular fitness (e.g., maximal oxygen uptake testing).

There are, however, validated alternatives such as the 1mile timed walk or computational estimates of cardiovascular fitness based on age, sex, body mass index, resting heart rate, and self-reported physical activity level (Jurca et al., 2005; McAuley et al., 2011).
text.formatted: There are, however, validated alternatives such as the 1mile timed walk or computational estimates of cardiovascular fitness based on age, sex, body mass index, resting heart rate, and self-reported physical activity level <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Jurca et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">McAuley et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions varied widely in their design and implementation.
For example, among screen-based exergame interventions, some used dance platform systems, while others employed motion-based systems such as the Nintendo Wii or Microsoft Xbox Kinect.

These systems differ in gameplay mechanics, user interaction styles, and likely engage different levels of physical and cognitive stimulation (Busser et al., 2024), which might impact their effect on EFs, as prior metaanalytic evidence suggests (Manser et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These systems differ in gameplay mechanics, user interaction styles, and likely engage different levels of physical and cognitive stimulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Busser et al., 2024)</ref>, which might impact their effect on EFs, as prior metaanalytic evidence suggests <ref type="bibr">(Manser et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We recommend that future exergame trials characterize their interventions using an established design or gamification taxonomy (e.g., feedback, progression, and social mechanics), thereby allowing future meta-analyses to test these features as moderators.
Standardized reporting of this kind would also advance the field by identifying which design characteristics are responsible for cognitive gains and in which populations.
Personalization and user-centered designs also warrant attention.
Tailoring exergames to the physical and cognitive needs of older users may increase both accessibility and efficacy (Torre & Temprado, 2022).
text.formatted: Tailoring exergames to the physical and cognitive needs of older users may increase both accessibility and efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Torre & Temprado, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Promising recent work has shown cognitive improvements among older adults with mild neurocognitive disorders using heart-rate biofeedback (Manser & de Bruin, 2024).
text.formatted: Promising recent work has shown cognitive improvements among older adults with mild neurocognitive disorders using heart-rate biofeedback <ref type="bibr">(Manser & de Bruin, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Further, closed-loop, adaptive technologies could dynamically adjust cognitive and physical difficulty, providing an optimal challenge tailored to individual capacity (Anguera et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Further, closed-loop, adaptive technologies could dynamically adjust cognitive and physical difficulty, providing an optimal challenge tailored to individual capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anguera et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The field would also benefit from longitudinal follow-up studies to assess the degree to which gains are maintained over time.

Only eight of the 48 studies in this review included followup assessments, leaving open questions about the persistence of cognitive gains and whether periodic "booster" sessions are necessary to maintain benefits.

Understanding the longevity and transferability of cognitive benefits from exergames would be essential for evaluating the longterm utility of exergames in cognitive aging and their impact, if any, on real-life outcomes.
Finally, the field may also benefit from moving toward open and updateable evidence syntheses that can evolve alongside the rapidly growing literature.
To facilitate this, the complete https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22756576 analytical framework to evolve as methodological standards develop.
text.formatted: To facilitate this, the complete <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22756576">dataset and analytical code underlying the present meta-analysis are publicly available at Zenodo's    repository, allowing the evidence base to be extended as new studies become available and the</ref> analytical framework to evolve as methodological standards develop.

text.text: The findings of the present meta-analysis indicate that, after accounting for publication bias, the evidence about the effects of exergames on cognition was inconclusive.
This pattern was consistent across sensitivity analyses, and no cognitive domain showed more than anecdotal evidence for an effect.
Likewise, there was no evidence that the effects differed by population or intervention characteristics.
These findings do not show that exergames are ineffective, but that the current evidence base does not allow to establish firm conclusions about their impact on cognition.

Since the apparent benefit of exergames largely depended on whether publication bias was taken into account, as the field continues to evolve, there is a pressing need for larger and well-powered preregistered trials.

Additionally, the use of standardized cognitive assessments, blinded outcome evaluation, adequately matched controls, and follow-up assessments, as well as mechanistic research will be essential to determine whether exergames can provide reliable and clinically meaningful cognitive benefits for middle-aged and older adults.

Finally, the rapid growth of exergaming research has been accompanied by increasing heterogeneity in intervention characteristics, study designs, cognitive outcome measures, and participant populations, which challenges the reproducibility and comparability of evidence syntheses.

Future systematic reviews and meta-analyses would therefore benefit from greater methodological standardization, including independent duplicate study selection and data extraction, transparent and reproducible classification of cognitive outcome domains, and the use of risk-of-bias tools matched to study design, such as RoB 2 for randomized controlled trials and ROBINS-I for non-randomized intervention studies (J. A.Sterne et al., 2016; J. A. C. Sterne et al., 2019).

text.text: Active control conditions should match exergames in engagement and expectation, ideally tested alongside passive control groups.
In the present literature, the type of group control was largely confounded with population characteristics, as alternative-treatment controls were used almost exclusively in clinical samples.
More RCTs conducted on clinical populations including both passive and alternative-treatment controls would help disentangle these factors.5.
Mechanistic research on exercise dose and intensity is also needed.

Future work should investigate the optimal dose of exergame interventions(Colcombe & Kramer, 2003), balancing session duration, frequency, and total training volume with considerations of fatigue and sustained motivation.

text.text: The role of type of exercise and exercise intensity on cognition deserves further attention.
